analysis.one_liner: Bans betting markets on US election outcomes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it was introduced in the Senate's final two weeks with zero cosponsors and referred to a committee that took no action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Commodity Exchange Act to stop any regulated exchange or clearinghouse from offering contracts, swaps, or other tradable instruments based on the outcome of political elections or contests [S2]. In practice, it would ban legalized betting markets on who wins elections. It was introduced on December 20, 2024, read twice, and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which is where election-gambling bills are routed because that committee oversees commodity futures regulation [S1]. No committee action, floor vote, or cosponsor ever followed, and the Congress ended days later [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and election officials benefit if the bill passes: it removes a mechanism by which wealthy bettors and political operatives could profit from election results, and it forecloses the appearance that election outcomes are a commodity to be traded. It also protects the integrity of election administration by reducing incentives for anyone to manipulate results or spreads doubt about them.

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits any agreement, contract, transaction, or swap involving a political election or contest from being listed or cleared on a regulated exchange, closing a legal channel for gambling on election outcomes [S2].
It applies to any index, measure, value, or data related to an election, so operators cannot get around the ban by trading on derivatives of results rather than results themselves [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Prediction-market platforms and any regulated exchanges that want to offer election contracts would lose a new line of business, and traders who want to bet on elections would lose a legal domestic venue. The public cost is minimal; the main trade-off is that some people believe markets help forecast outcomes.

drawbacks.text: The ban reaches only contracts 'listed or made available for clearing or trading on or through a registered entity' [S2], so it would not stop offshore or informal betting on elections, which would continue beyond US regulators' reach.
Supporters of election prediction markets argue they aggregate information and can be a useful forecasting tool; this bill eliminates that signal rather than regulating it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — keeping election outcomes from becoming a tradable financial product — is real and cheap, and it addresses a channel that opened in 2024 when a court allowed election contracts to trade. The main weaknesses are that the ban only covers regulated venues (pushing betting offshore rather than stopping it) and that it foregoes whatever forecasting value prediction markets provide. On balance the benefit to election integrity outweighs those costs, but the bill's design leaves obvious gaps.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with two weeks left in the Congress and sent to the Agriculture Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Merkley introduced the bill on December 20, 2024, near the end of the 118th Congress [S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day, and no further action of any kind was taken [S4].
The bill would have amended Section 5c(c)(5) of the Commodity Exchange Act to bar election-based contracts from registered exchanges and clearinghouses [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prediction-market operators and election bettors are better off because the bill died: legal betting on US elections on regulated venues was never shut down. No one in the general public gained anything from its failure.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 20, 2024, to ban election-based contracts on regulated exchanges; no other senator joined him

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 20, 2024, and took no further action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote or a floor fight: one Democrat sponsored the bill, no one else of either party signed on, and it never left committee.

industries.note: These platforms had begun offering, or sought to offer, contracts paying out on election results; the bill would end that business line on regulated venues. Election betting puts a cash price on political outcomes, which critics say invites manipulation and undermines public trust in elections.
The ban applies to contracts listed or cleared through registered entities under the Commodity Exchange Act [S2], removing election markets as a potential product for these venues.
